concept_html:
A model is calibrated when its probabilities mean what they say: of all customers scored 0.30, about 30% churn. Ranking metrics such as ROC AUC ignore calibration. A model can rank perfectly and still say 0.9 where the truth is 0.1.

Calibration matters whenever someone uses the number itself: expected revenue (probability × value), a forecast count of churners, a risk shown to a person, or thresholds agreed in probability terms.

Check it with a calibration table: group predictions into bins, then compare the mean predicted probability with the observed rate in each bin. scikit-learn 1.8 gives the same with calibration_curve(y, p, n_bins=10). Plot observed against predicted. A calibrated model follows the diagonal.

Summarise with the Brier score (brier_score_loss), the mean squared error of the probabilities. Compare it with a constant model that always predicts the prevalence.

A common cause of bad calibration is reweighting for imbalance. In this course's build, a logistic regression on data with 2.4% positives had a mean predicted probability of 0.024 and a Brier score of 0.021. The same model with class_weight="balanced" had a mean predicted probability of 0.42, and a Brier score of 0.199, worse than predicting 0.024 for everyone (0.024). Its AUC was slightly higher. Its probabilities were useless as probabilities.

Fix it with CalibratedClassifierCV(model, method="sigmoid", cv=5), which fits a calibration map on held-out folds. Use method="isotonic" only with plenty of data, roughly a thousand positives or more, because it overfits small samples. Check calibration again on the test set after fitting.

If you only need a ranking or a top-k list, calibration does not matter. Say which one you deliver.

lines: import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
def calibration_table(y: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, n_bins: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Mean predicted and observed rate per equal-width bin. Empty bins are left out."""
edges = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_bins + 1)
idx = np.searchsorted(edges[1:-1], p, side="right")
df = pd.DataFrame({"bin": idx, "y": y, "p": p})
table = df.groupby("bin").agg(mean_predicted=("p", "mean"), observed=("y", "mean"), n=("y", "size"))
return table.reset_index(drop=True)

exercises.solution:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd


def calibration_table(y: np.ndarray, p: np.ndarray, n_bins: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Mean predicted probability and observed rate per equal-width bin.

    Args:
        y: Binary outcomes.
        p: Predicted probabilities.
        n_bins: Number of equal-width bins on [0, 1].

    Returns:
        One row per non-empty bin: mean_predicted, observed, n.
    """
    edges = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_bins + 1)
    idx = np.searchsorted(edges[1:-1], p, side="right")
    df = pd.DataFrame({"bin": idx, "y": y, "p": p})
    table = df.groupby("bin").agg(mean_predicted=("p", "mean"), observed=("y", "mean"), n=("y", "size"))
    return table.reset_index(drop=True)

title: Calibration, when the probability itself matters
why_html: A retention team estimated campaign value as the sum of churn probabilities times customer margin. The model had been trained with balanced class weights. Its average churn probability was 0.41 on a base that churned at 3% a month. The business case promised ten times the saves the campaign could deliver, and budget was approved on it.
